summary: TypeScript gives you the type system Python's annotations only gesture at - and then erases every bit of it before the code runs. That is the whole shape of this transition: the compiler is genuinely good and the runtime underneath it is JavaScript, with one floating-point number type, string-only object keys, coercing `==`, and a `this` that falls off methods when you pass them around. The traps are not in the type system; they are in the gap between what the annotation promises and what the runtime does at the boundary where data actually arrives. Learn where the compiler stops checking - `as`, `any`, `JSON.parse`, array indexing - because that is exactly where your Python instincts will assume a runtime error that never comes.

verification.note: Snippets run against CPython 3.12.7, Node 23.1.0 and tsc 5.9.3 --strict.

concepts.title: Types vanish at runtime; `as` checks nothing
concepts.theirs: Annotations are also ignored at runtime, but you are used to that and you validate at the edges with pydantic, or you rely on the fact that a wrong type hits a TypeError fairly quickly because operators are strict.
concepts.yours: Types are erased entirely at compile time. `as User` is a claim you make to the compiler, not a conversion, and there is no `isinstance` to fall back on because the type does not exist at runtime.
concepts.trap: `const u = JSON.parse(body) as User` compiles clean under `--strict` and hands you an object whose id is the string "7" and whose name is undefined. Nothing raises. The string id flows into a comparison, `u.id === 7` is false, and the bug surfaces as a missing record. JavaScript's loose operators then keep it alive: `"7" * 2` is 14, so arithmetic on the wrong type often produces a plausible number. Validate at the boundary with zod or equivalent; treat every `as` in a diff as a place someone turned the compiler off.

concepts.title: `any` silently switches checking off, and strictness is a config choice
concepts.theirs: There is no `any`. An untyped Python function is untyped for everyone equally, and mypy's strictness settings do not change what the program does.
concepts.yours: `any` is assignable to and from everything, and it propagates through property access, calls and array elements. Without `strict` (specifically `noImplicitAny` and `strictNullChecks`) in tsconfig, untyped parameters become `any` and `null`/`undefined` are assignable to every type.
concepts.trap: One `any` at the edge - a library without types, a `catch (e)`, a hand-rolled fetch wrapper - disables checking for everything downstream of it, and the editor still shows confident-looking types the whole way. With `strictNullChecks` off, a `User` annotation is really `User | null | undefined`, so every red squiggle you were relying on for null safety was never turned on. Check tsconfig before you trust a codebase's types.

concepts.title: Indexing past the end returns undefined, and `-1` is not the last element
concepts.theirs: `lst[10]` on a short list raises IndexError immediately, and `lst[-1]` is the last element. Both behaviours are load-bearing in ordinary code.
concepts.yours: `arr[10]` returns undefined, and the declared type still says `number`. `arr[-1]` is a lookup of a property named "-1", so it is also undefined. The last element is `arr.at(-1)` or `arr[arr.length - 1]`.
concepts.trap: Both are silent under `--strict`: `const v: number = arr[10]` compiles and v is undefined at runtime, and any negative index you carried over from Python turns into undefined rather than wrapping. That undefined then survives - `undefined + 1` is NaN, JSON.stringify drops it from objects, and comparisons against it are quietly false - so the failure appears several layers from its cause. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` in tsconfig makes the compiler tell the truth about this; it is not part of `strict`.

concepts.title: There is one number type and it is a float64
concepts.theirs: int is arbitrary precision. A 19-digit id, a factorial, a hash - all exact, forever, with no configuration.
concepts.yours: `number` is an IEEE double. Integers are exact only up to 2**53 - 1. `bigint` exists with a separate literal syntax (`1n`) and does not mix with `number` in arithmetic.
concepts.trap: Precision is lost silently at the parse step, before any code of yours runs. `JSON.parse('{"id":9007199254740993}')` gives 9007199254740992, and the same is true of a literal typed into the source. Snowflake ids, Postgres bigints and nanosecond timestamps all land in that range, and the corruption is a single digit - the record still exists, it is just the wrong one. Carry large ids as strings across the wire.

concepts.title: `//` is a comment, not floor division
concepts.theirs: `a // b` floors and stays an int; `a / b` gives a float. Two distinct, visible operators.
concepts.yours: `/` is the only division and always produces a float: `7 / 2` is 3.5. Flooring is `Math.floor(a / b)`, and truncation toward zero is `Math.trunc`. `//` starts a line comment.
concepts.trap: `const mid = lo // 2` is not a syntax error. It parses as `const mid = lo`, with the rest of the line commented out and the semicolon inserted automatically. The variable is assigned - just to the un-divided value - so the code runs and a binary search or pagination offset is quietly wrong. Search a freshly ported file for `//` immediately after an identifier.

concepts.title: `%` on a negative number is negative
concepts.theirs: The result takes the sign of the divisor, so `-1 % 3` is 2 and `(i - 1) % len(xs)` is a correct backwards-cyclic index.
concepts.yours: The result takes the sign of the dividend, so `-1 % 3` is -1. The non-negative form is `((n % m) + m) % m`.
concepts.trap: The wrap-around idiom breaks at exactly one input. `xs[(i - 1) % xs.length]` works for every i except 0, where it evaluates to `xs[-1]` and yields undefined rather than the last element - so a carousel, ring buffer or round-robin scheduler misbehaves once per cycle and passes any test that starts in the middle. Hash bucketing has the same hole for negative hashes.

concepts.title: `[]` and `{}` are truthy
concepts.theirs: Empty containers are falsy, so `if items:` is the idiomatic non-empty check and `if not items:` covers both None and empty.
concepts.yours: Every object is truthy, including `[]` and `{}`. Only false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN are falsy. Non-empty is `items.length > 0`.
concepts.trap: `if (items)` is true for an empty array, so the "nothing to do" early return you relied on never fires and the code proceeds into a loop that does nothing, a UI that renders an empty table where the empty state should be, or a request sent with an empty payload. `if (!items)` has the same hole. It never raises, and it looks exactly like the Python you meant.

concepts.title: `===` on objects and arrays compares references
concepts.theirs: `==` on lists, dicts, tuples and dataclasses compares contents recursively, so `[1, 2] == [1, 2]` is True and value equality is the default assumption.
concepts.yours: `===` on objects and arrays is identity: `[1, 2] === [1, 2]` is false, and so is `{a: 1} === {a: 1}`. Structural comparison needs a helper - `assert.deepStrictEqual`, lodash `isEqual`, or a hand-written compare. `==` is worse, not better: it coerces, so `0 == ""` and `null == undefined` are both true.
concepts.trap: Every collection operation that leaned on value equality changes meaning at once, and none of them raise. `arr.includes(obj)`, `arr.indexOf(obj)` and `new Set(objects)` all compare by reference, so a Set of structurally identical objects deduplicates nothing and quietly grows. `Array.prototype.filter` with an equality predicate returns everything. Deduplicate on a primitive key, not on the object.

concepts.title: Object keys are strings; every object key collapses to the same one
concepts.theirs: Dict keys keep their type and hash by value. `d[1]` and `d["1"]` are different entries, and `d[(row, col)]` with a tuple key is an ordinary idiom.
concepts.yours: Plain-object keys are strings or symbols. Anything else is stringified on the way in. `Map` keeps key types and permits object keys - but compares those by reference, not by value.
concepts.trap: Two failures, both silent. `obj[1]` and `obj["1"]` are the same slot, so an id map fed both ints and strings merges entries. Worse, a tuple-key habit ported as `cache[[row, col]]` stringifies to "row,col" - which coincidentally works - while `cache[{row, col}]` stringifies to "[object Object]", so every single entry overwrites the previous one and the cache holds exactly one value while reporting hits for every key. Switching to `Map` fixes the type question and not the value-equality one: `m.set({a: 1}, x)` then `m.get({a: 1})` is undefined. Build a string key explicitly.

concepts.title: Methods lose their receiver when you pass them around
concepts.theirs: `obj.method` is a bound method that carries its instance permanently. Passing it as a callback is safe and common.
concepts.yours: `this` is determined by how the function is called, not where it was defined. Extracting `const f = obj.method` and calling `f()` leaves `this` undefined - class bodies are always strict mode. Arrow functions capture `this` lexically, which is why class properties are often declared as arrow functions.
concepts.trap: `setTimeout(this.flush, 1000)`, `arr.map(this.transform)` and `emitter.on('x', this.handle)` all compile, all type-check, and all throw "Cannot read properties of undefined" at call time - which is to say, later, in production, in whichever code path first triggers the callback. TypeScript will not catch it by default; `strictBindCallApply` does not cover this case. Pass `(...args) => this.handle(...args)`, or define the method as an arrow-function property.

concepts.title: A forgotten await gives you a truthy Promise
concepts.theirs: IO is synchronous by default. When you do use asyncio, a missing await means the coroutine never runs at all, which usually announces itself.
concepts.yours: An async function starts running immediately on call and returns a Promise. Every function that awaits anything must itself be async, so the colour spreads up the call stack.
concepts.trap: The work does happen - it just is not ordered or checked. A Promise object is always truthy, so `if (await?)` style guards pass: `if (userExists(id))` with the await forgotten is true even when the function resolves to false. A rejected Promise nobody awaited becomes an unhandled rejection that in Node 15 and later terminates the process by default, and a try/catch wrapped around an un-awaited call catches nothing. `array.forEach(async x => ...)` is the same bug in idiomatic clothing: forEach ignores the returned Promises and continues immediately, so use a `for...of` loop with await, or `Promise.all(array.map(...))`.

concepts.title: Types are structural, so distinct types with the same shape are interchangeable
concepts.theirs: isinstance and nominal classes. A UserId class and an OrderId class are never mistaken for each other, whatever their contents.
concepts.yours: A type is a shape. Anything with the required members satisfies it, no declaration or inheritance needed - which makes describing existing JavaScript pleasant, and makes two same-shaped types identical as far as the compiler is concerned.
concepts.trap: `type UserId = string` and `type OrderId = string` are aliases, not distinct types, so passing one where the other is expected type-checks perfectly and the mix-up shows up as a database miss. The same holds for `{lat: number, lng: number}` versus `{x: number, y: number}` once you rename fields. The fix is a branded type - `type UserId = string & {readonly __brand: unique symbol}` - which costs a cast at the boundary and buys real separation. Note that object *literals* do get an excess-property check, so the looseness is easy to underestimate from small examples.

concepts.title: Integer-like keys reorder themselves, and undefined disappears from JSON
concepts.theirs: Dicts preserve insertion order (guaranteed since 3.7) whatever the key types, and `json.dumps` writes them in that order. `None` serialises to null, and 3.0 serialises as 3.0.
concepts.yours: Object properties with integer-like string keys are ordered first, ascending, regardless of insertion order; everything else follows in insertion order. `JSON.stringify` omits keys whose value is undefined and turns undefined array elements into null. There is no float/int distinction, so 3.0 serialises as 3.
concepts.trap: `{b: 1, 2: 2, a: 3, 1: 4}` serialises as `{"1":4,"2":2,"b":1,"a":3}`. Anything that hashes or signs a JSON body - a webhook signature, an idempotency key, a cache key, a golden-file test - stops matching the Python side when keys happen to be numeric strings. Separately, a field set to undefined vanishes from the payload entirely rather than arriving as null, so a PATCH meant to clear a field instead leaves it untouched. Use null when you mean null.

concepts.title: `sort` compares as strings, and `replace` replaces once
concepts.theirs: `sorted(xs)` returns a new list and compares numbers as numbers; `list.sort()` mutates and returns None. `str.replace(a, b)` replaces every occurrence.
concepts.yours: `arr.sort()` mutates in place *and* returns the same array, and the default comparator converts each element to a string. Numeric sorting needs `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)`. `str.replace("a", "b")` with a string pattern replaces only the first match; `replaceAll` or a `/g` regex replaces all.
concepts.trap: Both fail by producing a result rather than an error. `[1, 10, 2, 9].sort()` returns [1, 10, 2, 9] - unchanged, and therefore extremely convincing - because "10" sorts before "2". And because sort returns the array, `const sorted = items.sort()` reads like the Python `sorted()` you meant while having also reordered the caller's array in place; use `[...items].sort()` if the original matters. The `replace` case gets caught in tests with one occurrence and escapes with two.
